name: TreeLine
workload: YCSB workloads (uniform and Zipfian key distributions, plus a real-world dataset) with 1024-byte records and read/scan/update mixes, run on an NVMe SSD
claimed_speedup: Outperforms RocksDB by 2.20x on average (16 threads, uniform); up to 2.50x on skewed (Zipfian) distributions; 1.62x on a real-world dataset
hardware: 20-core 2.10GHz Intel Xeon Gold 6230, 128GiB RAM, 1TB Intel DC P4510 NVMe SSD, Linux 5.12.5, ext4
tradeoffs: Update-in-place B+tree design targets modern NVMe SSDs specifically (random writes there approach sequential-write throughput); benefit is smaller or absent on HDD/SATA-SSD; RocksDB was run with compression and SSTable checksums disabled to match TreeLine's feature set, so this is not an out-of-the-box RocksDB comparison
caveats: VLDB'22 paper (peer-reviewed) does not state compiler or build flags, capping tier at B; repo has had no commits since Jan 2024

name: TidesDB
workload: benchtool suite: sequential/random/Zipfian writes, random reads, mixed read/write, single and batched deletes, seeks, range scans, batch-size scaling (1-10,000), and value-size sensitivity (64B-4KB), 8 threads; TidesDB v8.6.0 vs RocksDB v10.10.1
claimed_speedup: Faster than RocksDB on almost every test; geometric mean ~2.2x; sequential writes 4.97x (11.12M vs 2.24M ops/s), random reads 2.23x, Zipfian seeks ~5.3x, range scans up to 2.66x; RocksDB wins single-key deletes (RocksDB 971K vs TidesDB 603K ops/s) and batch-size-1 writes
compiler_and_flags: GCC (glibc); no version or optimization flags stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K (8 cores/16 threads) @ 4.9GHz, 48GB DDR4, WD Blue 500GB SATA SSD, Ubuntu 23.04 x86_64
tradeoffs: Uses roughly 4x more peak RSS memory than RocksDB (2,035MB vs 485MB) and higher CPU utilization (582% vs 258%) under write load; RocksDB still wins on single-key delete and batch-size-1 write throughput
caveats: First-party benchmark written by the TidesDB maintainer on the project's own blog, republished across many point-release versions; no independent third-party replication found; exact compiler version/flags and RocksDB tuning options not stated

name: VortexDB
workload: Single-node write/update/read/range-scan microbenchmark with ~8-byte keys and ~10-byte values, memtable size 10,000; compared against LevelDB v1.23 and, separately, SQLite v3.51.3 (individual and batched-transaction modes)
claimed_speedup: New-key writes: 550,221 ops/sec vs LevelDB's 188,175 ops/sec (~2.9x) and vs SQLite individual-transaction mode's 11,222 ops/sec (~49x, derived from page data); loses to LevelDB on read latency (0.06ms vs 0.0008ms) and range scans (6.58ms vs 0.17ms), and loses to SQLite's batched-transaction mode on writes/updates
hardware: Intel Core i5-12450HX, 12GB RAM @ 4800 MT/s, 512GB NVMe SSD, Windows 11 Home 64-bit
tradeoffs: WiscKey-style key/value separation wins on sequential new-key ingest (zero write amplification) but loses badly on point-read latency and range scans due to extra random VLog seeks; the update path forces an existence check that drops throughput ~11x versus new writes
caveats: Tiny single-author hobby project (3 stars); author transparently reports VortexDB losing on 3 of 5 measured operations against LevelDB; compiler/toolchain not stated; Windows-only test environment; results are self-reported in the project README with no independent verification

name: HSE (Heterogeneous-memory Storage Engine)
workload: YCSB 0.17.0 workloads A-D (load + run phases), 2TB dataset consisting of 2 billion 1,000-byte records, 96 client threads; HSE 1.7.0 vs RocksDB 6.6.4
claimed_speedup: Load phase: >8x RocksDB insert throughput (986,009 vs 122,899 inserts/sec), 88% shorter load duration, 99.9th-percentile insert latency 1.6ms vs 19.5ms; run phase up to ~6x more throughput across workloads A-D; tail latency reduced up to 91% for writes and 42% for reads; bytes written to SSD reduced by up to 85%
hardware: 2-socket Intel Xeon E5-2690 v4, 256GB DRAM, 4x Micron 9300 NVMe SSDs (3.2TB each, LVM striped), RHEL 8.1
stars_or_usage: 669 stars; integrated as a MongoDB storage engine (hse-mongo) and benchmarked via a public hse-ycsb fork
tradeoffs: Requires a dedicated 'mpool' storage-management layer and Micron-tuned NVMe configuration, adding operational complexity versus dropping in RocksDB; project (originated at Micron) has had no commits since August 2023
caveats: First-party vendor benchmark (HSE/Micron project docs), not independently reproduced; compiler and build flags not stated; project appears abandoned
